Fragmented Fandom

Baseball has always been a business, but the business has never been harder to navigate as a fan. This project follows one central question: as MLB finds more ways to monetize its games, how complicated and expensive does it become for fans to actually watch?

The story moves through five layers. First, the money: where national rights dollars flow and which partners now hold them. Second, the inventory: how many games land on each platform and what type of access each requires. Third, the fan budget: what it actually costs to assemble a full-season viewing stack. Fourth, the geography: how distance-based market logic compares to the real blackout restrictions MLB enforces. Fifth, a simple watchability model that synthesizes cost, platform count, and blackout risk into a single score per fan type.

All data was collected manually from public sources (MLB.com, team RSN disclosures, streaming platform pricing pages, and reported rights deal values). The fallback datasets embedded in this notebook reflect conditions as of the 2026 season.

2. Where Is the Money Going?

The modern MLB rights landscape is the product of a decade of incremental deals signed between 2018 and 2025. Fox and Turner (TBS) anchor the landscape with the two largest multi-year packages, both running through 2028. Apple TV+ entered in 2022 with a landmark streaming-exclusive deal that carries no blackout restrictions. NBC Universal and Netflix joined for 2026-2028, expanding the national footprint but also the number of services a completionist fan must subscribe to.

The two charts below tell complementary stories. The bar chart ranks partners by estimated annual value; the timeline shows which deals overlap during the same seasons, illustrating why the national package is now genuinely split across five different services simultaneously.

3. Where Are the Games Going?

Rights value tells us where the money flows. Game inventory tells us where the broadcast hours actually land. The chart below counts national games or events assigned to each package for the 2026 season.

One critical number is excluded from the chart: MLB.TV carries approximately 2,430 out-of-market games per season through its direct-to-consumer platform. That figure dwarfs every national package, but MLB.TV is a separate product subject to local blackout rules, so it is treated on its own in later sections.

The second chart reframes the same data by access type, answering the fan-level question: what kind of subscription do I actually need to watch these games?

4. What Can Fans Actually Watch?

This section translates the platform landscape into a fan budget. The question is not whether games exist on some service, but how many subscriptions a real fan needs to assemble, and what that stack costs per season.

Fan tier definitions used throughout this project:

Tier Description
Casual fan Free over-the-air broadcasts only (no paid subscription)
Basic cable fan One cable or live-TV bundle; relies on RSN for local games
Streaming-only fan Cord-cutter stack: Apple TV+, Peacock, Netflix
Out-of-market fan MLB.TV subscriber following a team outside their home region
Avid national fan Cable bundle plus streaming add-ons for broader national coverage
Completionist fan Every available service: cable + MLB.TV + Apple TV+ + Peacock + Netflix. Maximum access, maximum cost.

The scatter plot below adds a second dimension: dot size shows the number of services required, making the complexity cost visible alongside the dollar cost.

5. Following the Fan Over Time

Prices do not stay still. This section extends the fan-cost view back to 2022, the year Apple TV+ launched exclusive Friday Night Baseball, marking the first time a major streaming service held MLB rights with no cable or antenna path.

Three key inflection points shaped costs over this window. Apple TV+ launched at $4.99/month in April 2022 and rose to $17.99/month by early 2024. Peacock added select MLB games starting in 2023, requiring another subscription. And ESPN’s opt-out at the end of 2025 reshuffled national packages upward for the 2026 season.

The cheapest path (free OTA antenna) never changes. Every other path rises. The completionist fan’s annual bill grew by roughly $200 between 2022 and 2026 without any increase in the number of games watched.

6. How Do Markets Matter?

The geography of MLB fandom involves two competing logics that rarely agree. The first is distance: a fan nearest to a stadium belongs naturally to that market. The second is contract history: MLB blackout rules derive from RSN agreements signed decades ago, long before streaming geography existed.

Three views follow, each answering a different question.

  1. Thiessen (Voronoi) map - What would markets look like under pure distance logic? Labels anchor to each polygon’s interior via representative_point(), with nudges for dense corridors (NY, Chicago, SoCal, Bay Area, Florida).

  2. Side-by-side comparison - How does distance logic compare to actual MLB enforcement? Thiessen (left) beside the real blackout map (right). In the Mountain West the two maps look almost nothing alike.

  3. Interactive population choropleth - Where do fans actually live? County-level population overlaid on Thiessen territories shows which markets are geographically vast but demographically thin.

Interactive map: Population vs. Market Geography
The YlOrRd choropleth shows state population (darker = more people). Dashed white lines show each team's Thiessen (nearest-stadium) territory. Notice how the largest western territories span some of the least-populated states, yet their blackout zones reach just as far as any eastern market.

7. Can We Model Watchability?

The preceding sections each capture one dimension of the fan experience: cost, platform count, or blackout risk. This section combines all three into a single Watchability Index that summarizes how easy or difficult it is for each fan type to watch a full MLB season.

The index is constructed as a weighted composite. Blackout risk carries the most weight (45%) because it represents access uncertainty rather than just dollar cost. A fan can budget for a higher bill, but they cannot choose to be unblocked. Estimated cost carries 30% and platform count (complexity) carries 25%.

Higher scores mean easier access. The bar chart ranks fan types by their index score. The scatter plot shows the counterintuitive relationship between spending and watchability: paying more does not guarantee watching more.

8. Conclusion

MLB’s media landscape shows a clear tradeoff. More platforms create more revenue for the league, but they make the fan experience harder to navigate. A fan may need broadcast TV, a cable or live-TV bundle, standalone streaming subscriptions, and MLB.TV, while still facing blackout restrictions that can block games even after paying for a service.

The project’s central finding is that monetization and access do not move in the same direction. As MLB games spread across more rights partners, fans face higher complexity, higher potential cost, and less certainty about where their games can be watched.

Fan Recommendations

Fan Type Best Package Est. Cost Games Key Tip
Casual national fan Free OTA antenna + Apple TV+ ~$110/season ~51 local broadcast games Apple TV+ Friday Night Baseball has zero blackout rules and no cable required.
Local team fan YouTube TV or Hulu + Live TV ~$438-480/season ~162 team games via RSN Check RSN availability for your ZIP before subscribing. Diamond Sports collapse left some markets without a local option.
Out-of-market fan MLB.TV $149.99/season ~2,430 out-of-market games Always verify your ZIP-code blackout status at MLB.com before purchasing. Local blackout rules can still block your own team.
Completionist fan Cable + MLB.TV + Apple TV+ ~$650-750/season 2,600+ games Fox, TBS, and Apple TV+ cover all postseason rounds through 2028. Drop Peacock and Netflix to save without losing October.

Recommendation to MLB

Step 1 - Transparency: Build a publicly searchable, ZIP-code-level blackout tool so fans can see exactly which games are blacked out for their address before paying for any subscription. Currently, fans have no reliable way to know their blackout exposure until after they have already subscribed.

Step 2 - Reform: Cap multi-team blackout zones to a 75-mile radius from each stadium. Fans in the Mountain West and Great Plains can live 400+ miles from any MLB city and still be blacked out by multiple franchises due to overlapping historical RSN contracts. Narrowing these zones would close the gap between what fans pay and what they can actually watch, without dismantling the underlying rights structure.
